Your first study, Geier et al 2013, is a "hypothesis-generating" study. It's method is not a randomized control trial which could show causality. The hypothesis it puts forward is that thimerosal causes autism. Subsequent, much higher quality studies have shown clearly that it does not.

Your second study, Delong 2011, is a similar "hypothesis-generating" study. It's gated behind a paywall, so I can only evaluate the abstract. The last line is important. The author does not assert causation. She says further study is necessary.

Your third "study", Chhawchharia and Puliyel 2014, is not a study. It is an opinion published in an Indian journal of ethics.

Your fourth "study", Hooker et al 2014, is also not a study. It is an opinion and analysis of five, mostly older, studies. The 2nd of those studies is of particular interest because similar work has been done in 2010 and again in 2019 looking at all Danish children from the previous decades, and neither showed a positive correlation between thimerosal exposure and autism. These are high-quality studies of over 650,000 children.

Your fifth study, Singh et al 2002, is a molecular biology paper that shows that MMR vaccine produces antibodies. This is the intended function of the vaccine.
